article_title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
citation: Saptarshi Basu, Sandeep Kakar, Ashok Goel. (2026). A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402
title: Jill Watson prompt-engineering personalization module integrated with the RAG pipeline
description: A modular personalization component for the Jill Watson virtual teaching assistant that encodes learner attributes in an engineered prompt conditioning the underlying LLM at runtime. The article states it is "integrated with Jill Watson's retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and course-specific knowledge base, allowing personalization to modify the form and presentation of responses while preserving grounding in retrieved instructional content." It enables "scalable personalization without modifying or retraining the underlying LLM" and is designed for integration into the deployed Jill Watson architecture.
requirements: Learner preferences must be updatable through the Jill Watson interface and incorporated into prompts at runtime
A course-specific knowledge base and RAG pipeline must supply the shared instructional content
constraints: The module personalizes response form and presentation, not the retrieved content itself
Deployment integration is targeted for Spring 2027 with a Georgia Tech pilot in Summer 2027
target_learners: students in courses using the Jill Watson AI teaching assistant across institutions
target_learning_goals: course-grounded question answering tailored to individual learner preferences and question complexity
examples: Evaluated on 30 real student questions from the Spring 2023 CS 7637 KBAI course, generating 2,910 responses across 97 prompt configurations with GPT-4.1 at temperature 0
key_sources: Saptarshi Basu, Sandeep Kakar, Ashok Goel. (2026). A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402

article_title: Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet
citation: Marrs, K.A., and Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet. Cell Biology Education 3, 49–61. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.03-11-0022
title: JiTT: a feedback loop between Web-based pre-class assignments and classroom instruction
description: JiTT is a teaching and learning approach that combines traditional in-class instruction with Web communication. Its essence is a feedback loop: faculty post Warm Up assignments before class, students respond, and faculty use those responses to tailor the class session. As the authors state, "The essence of JiTT is the feedback loop between the Web and the classroom," emphasizing active learning, constructivism, and prompt feedback while decreasing traditional lecture.
requirements: Weekly Web-based Warm Up assignments due before class time
Faculty time before class to read and select student responses
A mechanism (CGI-bin or course management software) to collect and display student responses
constraints: JiTT is particularly useful in large enrollment courses and for commuting or part-time students, per the authors
target_learners: undergraduate nonscience majors in large-enrollment biology
advanced undergraduate biology majors and graduate students
target_learning_goals: addressing misconceptions and activating prior knowledge
active learning and cooperative problem solving
formative assessment and prompt feedback
examples: Contemporary Biology N100 (>200 students) and Biotechnology 540 (max 45 students) at IUPUI have used JiTT since 1999, teaching more than 1,000 biology students
key_sources: Marrs, K.A., and Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet. Cell Biology Education 3, 49–61. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.03-11-0022

article_title: Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet
citation: Marrs, K.A., and Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet. Cell Biology Education 3, 49–61. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.03-11-0022
title: JiTT lesson cycle: pre-class Warm Up, response-informed interactive lecture, cooperative learning, and post-class relevance essays
description: The article describes four common features structuring each week of a JiTT biology course: an online Dynamic Syllabus updated weekly, Web-based Warm Up assignments due 3 hours before class, an interactive classroom session combining lecture-discussion with cooperative learning exercises, and optional Good For relevance essays. The class session itself is split so that "a modified lecture-discussion is done for the first 3rd of the class, incorporating student Warm Up responses," followed by group work and a second lecture-discussion.
requirements: Warm Up responses collected and read before class so the lesson can be adjusted just in time
Cooperative learning exercises chosen to give hands-on experience with the concepts discussed
constraints: Contemporary Biology uses fixed auditorium-style seating, so groups form informally rather than by assignment
target_learners: undergraduate nonscience majors in large lecture courses
advanced undergraduate and graduate biology students
target_learning_goals: connecting instruction to student prior knowledge and misconceptions
active practice of course concepts during class
relevance and motivation
examples: In N100, informal groups of two to four students work 10–15 minutes on cooperative activities such as transcription/translation problems or graphing exercises
key_sources: Marrs, K.A., and Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet. Cell Biology Education 3, 49–61. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.03-11-0022

article_title: Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling
citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4
title: Collaborative multidisciplinary modeling task combining Jigsaw grouping with knowledge-building pedagogy
description: A unit-level design in which students first work in disciplinary groups (biology, chemistry, physics) to investigate a phenomenon and build disciplinary models, then are rearranged into multidisciplinary groups of one student per discipline who share models and develop a collaborative combined model. The Jigsaw approach "ensured symmetric knowledge advancement, as each participant acted as a disciplinary expert and was essential to the group's progress". The shared model serves as an epistemic artifact that triggers advancement of interdisciplinary knowledge in the classroom community, following knowledge-building principles such as idea improvement, diversity of perspectives, and epistemic agency.
requirements: Students with different disciplinary expertise who each contribute a disciplinary model
An authentic, real-world problem that resonates with students' lived experiences
Extended time for collaborative work (the unit comprised four learning sets and 15 lessons of 45 min each, some double periods)
constraints: Due to COVID-19 pandemic, students completed the unit online and used online tools (draw.io) to develop their models
target_learners: high school students majoring in different scientific disciplines
target_learning_goals: collaborative sense-making of a scientific phenomenon
integrating disciplinary perspectives into a shared model
examples: The unit How does alcohol consumption affect our body? had students develop disciplinary models of alcohol's effects, then combine them into multidisciplinary models and write final reports reflecting on the process
key_sources: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4

article_title: Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later
citation: Eva Vives, Céline Poletti, Anaïs Robert, Fabrizio Butera, Pascal Huguet, et al.. (2024). Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241230064
title: The jigsaw classroom as a cooperative learning method designed to improve minority children's performance by reducing intergroup conflict and increasing self-evaluations
description: The jigsaw classroom is a cooperative learning method originating in the late 1970s. According to the review, it was "designed in the late 1970s to improve the academic performance of minority children by reducing intergroup conflict and increasing self-evaluations." The method rests on social interdependence and collaboration, and its intended mechanisms are simultaneously academic (performance) and psychosocial (intergroup relationships, self-evaluations). This review is the first systematic synthesis of the evidence base for the method across more than 40 years of research.
requirements: Implementation as a cooperative learning activity structured to reduce intergroup conflict and raise self-evaluations, per the method's original design aims
constraints: The review notes that despite high popularity, the available evidence for effectiveness seems scant and mixed
target_learners: Minority children in classroom settings (original design population); learners across academic subjects in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Academic performance across subjects
Intergroup relationships
Self-evaluations
examples: The review synthesized 69 studies of the method conducted from 1978 through 2022
key_sources: Eva Vives, Céline Poletti, Anaïs Robert, Fabrizio Butera, Pascal Huguet, et al.. (2024). Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241230064

article_title: Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later
citation: Eva Vives, Céline Poletti, Anaïs Robert, Fabrizio Butera, Pascal Huguet, et al.. (2024). Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241230064
title: Systematic review corpus of 69 jigsaw studies (1978–2022)
description: The evidence base assembled by this review: a systematic search covering studies "conducted from 1978 through 2022" that assessed "the effects of jigsaw on both academic performance and psychosocial variables (e.g., intergroup relationships, self-evaluations)." Sixty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria, making this the first systematic review of the method — prior to it there was "neither meta-analysis nor systematic review." The corpus underpins the review's conclusions about overall positive effects and their variation across subjects and outcome variables.
requirements: Studies had to meet the review's inclusion criteria and address jigsaw effects on academic performance and/or psychosocial variables
constraints: Limited to studies conducted from 1978 through 2022
target_learners: Learners in the 69 included jigsaw studies, spanning classroom settings and academic subjects
target_learning_goals: Academic performance
Psychosocial variables including intergroup relationships and self-evaluations
examples: The review screened more than four decades of jigsaw research and retained 69 studies
key_sources: Eva Vives, Céline Poletti, Anaïs Robert, Fabrizio Butera, Pascal Huguet, et al.. (2024). Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241230064

article_title: Cooperative learning reduces the gender gap in perceived social competences: A large-scale nationwide longitudinal experiment.
citation: Rudmann, O., Batruch, A., Visintin, E. P., Sommet, N., Bressoux, P., Darnon, C., ... Butera, F. (2023). Cooperative Learning Reduces the Gender Gap in Perceived Social Competences. A Large-Scale Nationwide Longitudinal Experiment. Journal of Educational Psychology (accepted for publication). https://osf.io/qarxk/?view_only=e772332576a5421cbf61b3092e567ac9
title: Jigsaw classroom as cooperative learning with positive goal and resource interdependence
description: The Jigsaw classroom is a cooperative learning method in which "each group member possesses a unique portion of the learning materials" and all members pursue the same goal, creating positive goal and resource interdependence. In the ProFAN experiment it was implemented in five stages: Jigsaw groups of 3-5 students each study a sub-section, meet in expert groups, return to present their sub-section, and produce a collective assignment requiring articulation of all sub-sections. The article positions this structure as what allows all students to practice social competences.
requirements: Each student must feel responsible for attaining their learning goal as well as helping groupmates attain the same goal
A unique portion of the learning materials must be distributed to each group member so resources must be combined
constraints: Some criticism has recently emerged about the effectiveness of this method as far as performance and achievement are concerned
target_learning_goals: social competences such as communication, collaboration, and collective problem solving
examples: In the ProFAN experiment students went four times through three pedagogical sequences (12 sequences over two years) under the Jigsaw method in 108 French vocational high schools
key_sources: Rudmann, O., Batruch, A., Visintin, E. P., Sommet, N., Bressoux, P., Darnon, C., ... Butera, F. (2023). Cooperative Learning Reduces the Gender Gap in Perceived Social Competences. A Large-Scale Nationwide Longitudinal Experiment. Journal of Educational Psychology (accepted for publication). https://osf.io/qarxk/?view_only=e772332576a5421cbf61b3092e567ac9

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Jingle-jangle fallacies as a construct-validation framework for positive self-belief measures
description: The article re-introduces Kelley's classic jingle-jangle fallacies as a construct-validation framework: a jingle fallacy occurs when 'two scales with similar names might measure different constructs', and a jangle fallacy when 'apparently dissimilar labels might measure similar constructs'. The framework prescribes testing convergent and discriminant validity with CFA, SEM, and multitrait-multimethod logic, using frame-of-reference effects and longitudinal prediction of outcomes as validation criteria. The authors apply it to five math self-belief measures.
requirements: Construct validity studies comparing multiple candidate measures in a single factor analysis are needed, because a scale loading on one factor alone does not test discriminant validity against other constructs
constraints: Scale labels alone are not sufficient evidence of how a scale relates to other constructs
target_learning_goals: academic self-beliefs and motivation in mathematics
examples: The authors classify five math self-belief measures a priori as self-concept-like or self-efficacy-like and test that classification empirically
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281

article_title: Do jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis.
citation: Arnaud Stanczak, Céline Darnon, Anaïs Robert, Marie Demolliens, Camille Sanrey, Pascal Bressoux, Pascal Huguet, Céline Buchs, Fabrizio Butera, and PROFAN Consortium. (2022). Do Jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (6), pp.1461-1476. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000730
title: The classical three-step jigsaw procedure: jigsaw groups on subtopics, expert groups, then teaching back to the jigsaw group
description: This pattern structures positive interdependence by distributing complementary resources among group members across three steps. As the article describes it, "In the jigsaw classroom, students work in groups on pedagogical content divided into several subtopics. The classical procedure usually follows three major steps": students first work individually on their assigned subtopic, then meet in expert groups with peers who studied the same subtopic to check understanding, then return to their jigsaw groups and take turns teaching their topic to the other members. In the experiments, this procedure was compared against individualistic or teaching-as-usual conditions on identical content.
requirements: Pedagogical content divided into subtopics with complementary resources distributed so each member is responsible for explaining one part
Expert-group meetings so students can check understanding before teaching back
constraints: The article reports that the three-step procedure "generates different dynamics between members", with the expert step linked to individualistic dynamics and the jigsaw step involving both positive and negative dynamics
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes across mathematics, life and earth sciences, physics and chemistry
examples: Experiment 3A adapted a physics-chemistry topic into jigsaw subtopics where expert groups tested specific predictions (e.g., mass conservation with sugar, sand, salt, or vinegar in water) and reported results back to their jigsaw groups
key_sources: Arnaud Stanczak, Céline Darnon, Anaïs Robert, Marie Demolliens, Camille Sanrey, Pascal Bressoux, Pascal Huguet, Céline Buchs, Fabrizio Butera, and PROFAN Consortium. (2022). Do Jigsaw classrooms improve learning outcomes? Five experiments and an internal meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (6), pp.1461-1476. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000730

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8
title: JIT and VIZ personalized feedback modules with two granularity levels and timeline visualization
description: The E-portfolio environment is enhanced with "a feedback module providing personalized improvement feedback (JIT module)" and "a visualization module that visualizes the feedback in terms of the personal development over time (VIZ module)". Feedback is provided at two granularity levels: aggregated messages (improvement, positive/negative, supervisor, trend, cohort, gaps) and detailed feedback with concrete improvement suggestions accessible by clicking. The interactive graph is a timeline with coloured trend lines per EPA, assessment dots placed by date and aggregated score, with pop-up boxes for assessment summaries and narrative JIT feedback.
requirements: The modules communicate with the E-portfolio and student model via Rest APIs, with anonymized data updates and a central authentication server for secure authentication
constraints: Experts noted it was not always clear when elements in the VIZ module are interactive, and suggested options for colour blindness and black-and-white printing
target_learners: students in professional education and their supervisors
target_learning_goals: self-assessment, monitoring progress on EPAs and competencies, improvement of performance
examples: Stakeholder meetings with 46 students and supervisors shaped the feedback categories: notifications, content feedback and longitudinal feedback, with both quantitative and qualitative feedback preferred in a simple overview
key_sources: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8

article_title: Which One Is Better? Jigsaw II versus Jigsaw IV on the Subject of the Building Blocks of Matter and Atom
citation: Turkmen, H. & Buyukaltay, D. (2015). Which one is better? Jigsaw II versus Jigsaw IV on the subject of the building blocks of matter and atom. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(2), 88-94. https://www.jeseh.net
title: Jigsaw technique step structure and the Jigsaw II / Jigsaw IV variant differences
description: The article describes the jigsaw technique as a cooperative learning procedure in which students are divided into 3-7 person jigsaw groups, the subject is divided into segments, students meet in expert groups to learn their segment, return to their jigsaw groups to teach it, and finally take an individual quiz. Drawing on Holliday (2002), it tabulates nine steps and identifies that "Jigsaw II and Jigsaw IV techniques diverse in 1 st, 4th, 6th, 7th and 9th steps": Jigsaw IV adds a teacher-led introduction, an expert-group accuracy check, a second whole-material test, a whole-class review, and optional re-teaching of missed material.
requirements: Students are divided into 3-7 person jigsaw groups and the subject is divided into segments
Expert groups work together before returning to home teams to teach their segments
constraints: The ninth-step re-teaching practice is optional and unnecessary when students have gained the required behaviors
target_learning_goals: science content achievement on the atoms and basic units of matter topic
examples: In the study, the experiment group followed the Jigsaw IV program and the control group the Jigsaw II program, both over two weeks with heterogeneous groups of 6 students
key_sources: Turkmen, H. & Buyukaltay, D. (2015). Which one is better? Jigsaw II versus Jigsaw IV on the subject of the building blocks of matter and atom. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(2), 88-94. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105340

article_title: The Effect of Jigsaw Technique on the Students' Laboratory Material Recognition and Usage Skills in General Physics Laboratory-I Course
citation: Abdullah Aydin, Filiz Biyikli. (2017). The Effect of Jigsaw Technique on the Students' Laboratory Material Recognition and Usage Skills in General Physics Laboratory-I Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(7). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050701
title: Jigsaw technique as a two-group cooperative learning structure with expert teaching roles
description: The article describes jigsaw as a cooperative learning structure in which "students are members of two different groups, the 'home group' and the 'jigsaw group'." Students first learn an assigned portion of the material as experts in jigsaw groups with peers from other home groups, then return to home groups to teach their portion. In this study the six physics laboratory experiments defined the six expert portions, and the structure was credited with making each student responsible for teaching material to the group.
requirements: Each member must be assigned a distinct portion of the material to learn and later teach
Members should be informed about their responsibilities, per the authors' conclusions
constraints: The authors state it is not recommended for very crowded classes due to difficulty in controlling the class
target_learners: science-education teacher candidates in university physics laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: recognition and use of physics laboratory materials
laboratory experiment skills
understanding of experiment subtopics
examples: Six main groups were formed around the six experiments (e.g., Speed and Acceleration, Free Fall, Simple Pendulum); jigsaw groups of six to seven students then prepared teaching strategies for their subtopics before returning to home groups as expert students
key_sources: Abdullah Aydin, Filiz Biyikli. (2017). The Effect of Jigsaw Technique on the Students' Laboratory Material Recognition and Usage Skills in General Physics Laboratory-I Course. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(7). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050701

article_title: The Effect of Self-Regulated Jigsaw IV on University Students' Academic Achievements and Attitudes towards English Course
citation: Esin Özdemir, Ali Arslan. (2016). The Effect of Self-regulated Jigsaw IV on University Students' Academic Achievements and Attitudes towards English Course. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i5.1453
title: Jigsaw IV nine-phase cooperative learning sequence
description: Jigsaw IV is a cooperative learning technique developed by Holliday in the late 1990s in which each student's part is essential to the group product, as with a jigsaw puzzle. The article prints its implementation as "nine phases (Holliday, 2002)", moving from teacher introduction and task distribution, through expert-group and home-group work with quizzes at each stage, to individual assessment and reteaching of material not adequately explored. In this study the technique was combined with self-regulated learning strategies such as group goal setting and intermittent self-evaluation.
requirements: Teacher introduces the material and distributes tasks to home groups
Expert groups and home groups work collaboratively with quizzes at each stage
target_learning_goals: learning a new grammar structure (modals) in English
examples: In the experimental group, students in home groups made plans together, set common goals, took tests and evaluation forms to compare performance with goals, and adjusted strategies as needed
key_sources: Esin Özdemir, Ali Arslan. (2016). The Effect of Self-regulated Jigsaw IV on University Students' Academic Achievements and Attitudes towards English Course. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i5.1453

article_title: Effect of Jigsaw I Technique on Teaching Turkish Grammar
citation: Akif ARSLAN. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw I technique on teaching Turkish grammar. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2709
title: Jigsaw I cooperative learning technique
description: Jigsaw I is a cooperative learning method, developed by Aronson et al. (1978), in which "interdependency is created" through original and expert groups. Students in original groups of 2-6 research assigned sub-topics, meet in expert groups with students researching the same topic, then return to original groups and teach their expertise to peers before an individually scored test. In this study it was applied to three weeks of Turkish spelling and punctuation topics in grade 8.
requirements: Students must be prepared and trained for cooperative learning before the technique is applied
constraints: The article notes taking extra time and being not appropriate for grade one students as negative aspects of the technique
target_learning_goals: Turkish grammar: spelling rules and punctuation marks
examples: Five original groups (A-E) of six coded members met expert groups by topic code across three weekly cycles of topic assignment, expert-group study, and original-group peer teaching
key_sources: Akif ARSLAN. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw I technique on teaching Turkish grammar. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2709

article_title: The Effects of Jigsaw Technique Based on Cooperative Learning on Prospective Science Teachers' Science Process Skill
citation: Ataman Karacop, Emine Hatun Diken. (2017). The Effects of Jigsaw Technique Based on Cooperative Learning on Prospective Science Teachers' Science Process Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Jigsaw laboratory cycle: heterogeneous home groups plus expert groups alternating around shared experiments
description: The article's Jigsaw implementation organises a 15-week laboratory course into five-person heterogeneous Jigsaw groups formed by academic achievement, and topic-based expert groups of the same size. Each member studies one sub-topic, performs its related experiments, and teaches it back in the home group before all groups run experiments by turns. The article reports that "five Jigsaw groups with five people w ere formed" and "five Expert Groups consisting of f ive members were set up", with 2 hours for first Jigsaw activities, 4 for expert groups, 4 for second Jigsaw activities and 10 for experiments per field.
requirements: The main content chosen for group work must be divided into sub-categories for the equal responsibility of group members
Cooperative tasks must be challenging enough to require joint effort and include sufficient tasks for each member to contribute
constraints: When students believe their individual efforts are not related to group performance, social evasion and fool effect may occur
Some student teachers' not doing their job properly affected other student teachers' learning badly
target_learners: third-grade prospective science teachers in tertiary education
target_learning_goals: scientific process skills
physics, chemistry and biology laboratory content
cooperative social skills
examples: Five Jigsaw groups and five expert groups were tracked across Physics, Biology and Chemistry fields, each application completed in 5 weeks (20 class hours)
key_sources: Ataman Karacop, Emine Hatun Diken. (2017). The Effects of Jigsaw Technique Based on Cooperative Learning on Prospective Science Teachers' Science Process Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1133003

article_title: The Effect of Using Jigsaw Strategy in Teaching Science on the Acquisition of Scientific Concepts among the Fourth Graders of Bani Kinana Directorate of Education
citation: Dr. Qaseem Mohammad Salim Hamadneh. (2017). The Effect of Using Jigsaw Strategy in Teaching Science on the Acquisition of Scientific Concepts Among the Fourth Graders of Bani Kinana Directorate of Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.5. https://www.iiste.org
title: Jigsaw cooperative learning: expert-part groups each master a content part and teach it back to build the full picture
description: The Jigsaw strategy organizes students into small groups of 5-6 members where "each student is give n information that is not give n to another in the g roup making him an expert in the part of the subject". Experts from different groups meet to study a part, then return to teach their home groups, so the parts are organized into one full image. The article applies this pattern to fourth-grade science units and credits it with inter-reliability, whereby team members rely on each other during performance.
requirements: Students must each receive a distinct part of the content and be prepared to teach their own subject after mastering it
constraints: The article's procedural definition ties the pattern to small groups of 5-6 members with degrees or other rewards granted
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific concepts in science units
examples: The researcher designed teaching methods using Jigsaw for fourth-grade science lessons, had them reviewed by 8 specialized arbitrators, and taught the experimental group through them while the control group used the traditional textbook method.
key_sources: Dr. Qaseem Mohammad Salim Hamadneh. (2017). The Effect of Using Jigsaw Strategy in Teaching Science on the Acquisition of Scientific Concepts Among the Fourth Graders of Bani Kinana Directorate of Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.5. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1133045

article_title: Effect of Jigsaw Technique and Gender on Students' Attitude to Ethnic Integration and Sustainable Development in Nigeria
citation: Ajitoni Sunday Olukayode & Salako, Ekima Tina. (2014). Effect of Jigsaw Technique and Gender on Students' Attitude to Ethnic Integration and Sustainable Development in Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n3p46
title: Jigsaw technique as a cooperative learning method built on five elements of positive interdependence and interaction
description: The article presents jigsaw as a cooperative learning technique in which students are organised into groups "mixed as heterogeneously as possible", first by academic ability and then by ethnic background, race, and gender, with each student responsible for teaching part of the subject. Following Machaisa (2004) and Kagan (2001), it identifies the elements of jigsaw as "positive interdependence, promotive face-to-face interaction, individual accountability, social skills, and group processing", which the authors call germane to promoting peaceful co-existence in society.
requirements: Groups must be mixed as heterogeneously as possible, first by academic abilities and then by ethnic backgrounds, race, and gender
Each student must take responsibility to teach a part of the subject
constraints: The article notes obstacles such as student dominance, addressed by appointing a group leader, and possible boredom among bright students
target_learning_goals: attitudes of ethnic integration and respect for other cultures
cooperation and social skills
examples: In the study, 126 junior secondary students were taught a multicultural education curriculum package in jigsaw or conventional groups and compared on attitude post-test scores
key_sources: Ajitoni Sunday Olukayode & Salako, Ekima Tina. (2014). Effect of Jigsaw Technique and Gender on Students' Attitude to Ethnic Integration and Sustainable Development in Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n3p46

article_title: Use of Jigsaw Technique to Teach the Unit "Science within Time" in Secondary 7th Grade Social Sciences Course and Students' Views on This Technique
citation: Hakkı Yapıcı. (2016). Use of jigsaw technique to teach the unit "science within time" in secondary 7th grade social sciences course and students' views on this technique. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(8), 773-780. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR
title: Jigsaw implementation pattern: home groups, expert subtopics, and peer teaching within a five-week unit
description: The article implements jigsaw by dividing the class into five home groups of five students, each assigned one main subject of the unit. Each member researches a subtopic, meets in jigsaw groups with peers holding the same subtopic, then returns to teach it to home-group members. The class was "divided into five groups. Each group was formed by five students", covering Geographical Discoveries, Renaissance, Reform, Age of Enlightenment, and Industrial Revolution.
requirements: Each group member is given a subtopic to research, learn, and teach to other group members
Groups choose a title and president; materials and roles are prepared in advance
constraints: The unit was taught three hours a week over five weeks by the researcher; the article recommends the method only where there are enough resources and time
target_learning_goals: social sciences content knowledge of the "Science within Time" unit
examples: Home groups chose titles such as 'Virgos' and 'Tauruses'; students in A1-E1 researched causes and results of geographical discoveries, then taught their subtopics in home-group lessons in the third week
key_sources: Hakkı Yapıcı. (2016). Use of jigsaw technique to teach the unit "science within time" in secondary 7th grade social sciences course and students' views on this technique. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(8), 773-780. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR

article_title: Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool
citation: Nilüfer Okur Akçay. (2016). Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n3p83
title: Jigsaw structure for preschoolers: five-person basic groups, five expert topics, expert groups, then return and joint product
description: The article describes a concrete jigsaw implementation for four-to-five-year-olds: "four basic groups each of which consisted of five people was formed", the sense-organs content was split into five titles (ear, nose, tongue, eye, skin), each child researched one title and taught it to group mates, then students regrouped into expert jigsaw groups to present their title, and finally returned to their basic groups to teach and build a joint product. The teacher guided, supplied materials, and organized experiments, games and riddles throughout.
requirements: A teacher presentation on how to study, responsibilities and rules before group work begins
Each group determines a group name and a group leader
The teacher determines materials and undertakes a guidance role to help the groups
constraints: Implemented with four-to-five-year-old nursery children on a single science topic (sense organs) over about a week of expert teaching
target_learners: preschool children aged four to five
target_learning_goals: knowledge of sense organs (ear, nose, tongue, eye, skin) and their functions (hearing, smelling, tasting, seeing, touching/sensing)
examples: Students attached mixed organs to a human model, painted them, and placed appropriate senses on the organs as a joint work after each child taught their expert topic for a week
key_sources: Nilüfer Okur Akçay. (2016). Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n3p83

article_title: The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill
citation: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://www.iiste.org
title: Just In Time Teaching (JITT) strategy
description: JITT is a strategy that "combines the use of information technology and act ive learning in the classroom that is feedback between students and lecturers so as to encourage l earning-centered student". Students complete web-delivered pre-class assignments, which lets the lecturer identify strengths, weaknesses and learning styles before face-to-face class and streamlines classroom time for inquiry activities. In this study JITT phases were embedded into the first two phases of the Inquiry Training model.
requirements: Web-based delivery of pre-class assignments and review material
Feedback loop between students and lecturer before direct classroom learning
target_learning_goals: efficient use of classroom time
student-centred learning
problem-solving skill development
examples: Problems to be solved were given on the web so students had ample time to seek solutions to test or present during inquiry class
key_sources: Betty Turnip, Ida Wahyuni, Yul Ifda Tanjung. (2016). The Effect of Inquiry Training Learning Model Based on Just in Time Teaching for Problem Solving Skill. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103095

article_title: Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine
citation: Sanqiang Pan, Xin Cheng, Yanghai Zhou, Ke Li & Xuesong Yang. (2017). Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine. International Journal of Higher Education, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v6n1p25
title: Elective vertical integrated courses on cardiovascular and respiratory systems (Jinan University, 2012)
description: Two 45-hour elective vertical integrated courses offered to year 1 and year 3 medical undergraduates during summer vacation 2012, integrating basic sciences and clinical medicine by organ system. Teaching approaches "consisted of intern, lectures, demonstration and PBL," with lecturers from both basic and clinical disciplines trained in PBL by University of Hong Kong teachers, and course content modeled on curricula from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and Shantou University.
requirements: Lecturers from different disciplines previously trained by PBL-experienced teachers
Participants selected with average scores at or above 82 (Grade B)
constraints: Offered as elective courses during summer vacation so the normal teaching schedule was not disturbed
target_learning_goals: integrating basic science with clinical medicine
clinical case analysis
examples: The cardiovascular course included coronary heart disease, hypertension and heart failure content with two PBL sessions on coronary atherosclerosis; the respiratory course covered bronchiogenic carcinoma, pneumonia and pleural effusion with two PBL sessions
key_sources: Sanqiang Pan, Xin Cheng, Yanghai Zhou, Ke Li & Xuesong Yang. (2017). Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine. International Journal of Higher Education, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v6n1p25

article_title: Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China
citation: Xiaoye Lu, Xin Cheng, Ke Li, Kenneth Ka Ho Lee & Xuesong Yang. (2016). Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p157
title: Pilot integrated histology theory-and-practice curriculum at Jinan University School of Medicine
description: A pilot curriculum for overseas-enrolled Clinical Medicine students in which histology theory teaching was implemented simultaneously with laboratory demonstration, designed to remove the temporal-spatial barrier of the traditional separated format. The content, textbook, examination papers and graders were identical to the traditional course; only delivery differed. It was taught twice weekly in 120-minute sessions totalling 108 hours (54 lecture, 54 practice).
requirements: Morphology laboratories with histology slides, light microscopes, computers with digital panorama imaging system and internet access for every student; more tutors needed to scale up
constraints: Voluntary participation of 24 of 69 students; laboratory capacity limits hosting; teachers reported needing more preparation time than traditional teaching
target_learners: sophomore overseas Chinese students of Clinical Medicine
target_learning_goals: comprehension of histological theory and its application during microscope practice
examples: 24 students voluntarily joined the pilot while the remaining 45 non-participants acted as the control group.
key_sources: Xiaoye Lu, Xin Cheng, Ke Li, Kenneth Ka Ho Lee & Xuesong Yang. (2016). Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p157

article_title: Just-in-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities
citation: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65
title: Just-in-time teaching as a web-mediated feedback loop between out-of-class preparation and classroom instruction
description: The article presents JiTT as a teaching and learning strategy combining classroom activities that promote active learning with web resources. Its "essential element is feedback between the web-based and classroom activities": students complete web-based preparatory assignments due a few hours before class, submit them electronically, and the teacher adjusts lessons in response to these just-in-time submissions. The cycle recurs several times weekly in short sessions to avoid fatigue.
requirements: Web-based preparatory assignments submitted electronically before class
Teacher review of submissions to adjust and organize classroom lessons
target_learners: vocational certificate students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: English reading ability
English writing ability
positive attitudes toward learning English
examples: The experimental treatment implemented JiTT across ten phases, from warm-up exercises via an online discussion board through teamwork, communication, and an interactive lecture culminating in a restaurant brochure task.
key_sources: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65

article_title: Just-in-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities
citation: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65
title: Ten-phase JiTT lesson sequence for English reading and writing with vocational students
description: The article operationalizes JiTT through web technologies as a ten-phase lesson sequence: warm-up exercise/motivation, classroom setting with real-world connection, traditional assignments for critical thinking, estimation, defining problems, teamwork, communication, time management, recitation dealing with new vocabularies, and interactive lecture. Phases alternate online work (discussion boards, web searches, Gmail submissions) with teacher-led group discussion, feedback, and paragraph writing on food and eating-habits topics.
requirements: Online discussion board and web-based tools for gathering student responses
Teacher feedback and advice between phases
Group organization for collaborative tasks
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of printed media texts
paragraph writing in English
vocabulary development
examples: In Phase 2 students picked restaurant types and located websites with menus; in Phase 7 students sent online practice pages with Gmail and the teacher checked JiTT responses in an online discussion area.
key_sources: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65

article_title: Just-in-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities
citation: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65
title: Extend JiTT through web technologies to other language skills and design materials that support independent searching
description: In its recommendations the article states that although the study targeted reading and writing, "it could be extended to support other language skills," and that teachers should willingly explore teaching materials, audio-visual aids, and equipment so students develop independent searching according to their interests and attitudes. JiTT through web technologies can also connect students with educational resources and collaborative learning communities outside the classroom.
requirements: Teacher willingness to explore teaching materials, audio-visual aids, and equipment
Web technology access for connecting students with educational resources
constraints: The article notes materials should be designed especially to assist students in learning English for understanding and to practice other language activities.
target_learning_goals: independent searching and studying
other language skills beyond reading and writing
examples: The authors suggest figuring out how to emphasize helping students learn in other subject areas with specially designed materials.
key_sources: Rewadee Chantoem & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2016). Just-In-Time Teaching Techniques through Web Technologies for Vocational Students' Reading and Writing Abilities. English Language Teaching, 9(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p65

article_title: The Impact of Teaching the Subjects under "Science in Time" Unit in the Social Studies Class in the 7th Grade Using Jigsaw Technique on the Academic Success of the Students
citation: Harun Er. (2017). The Impact of Teaching the Subjects under "Science in Time" Unit in the Social Studies Class in the 7th Grade Using Jigsaw Technique on the Academic Success of the Students. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(5): 838-847. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050516
title: Jigsaw two-stage group structure: primary groups study distributed topics, expert groups consolidate, then members teach each other
description: The jigsaw technique organizes a class into small "primary" groups of 3-7 students, each assigned a topic from the same unit; members then regroup into "expertise" groups with peers responsible for the same topic before returning to teach their primary groups. The article describes that "Every individual leaves his/her primary group after studying the topic s/he is responsible for, form the groups, called “expertise”", after which members "are responsible for telling and teaching the topics, they have prepared, to each other" and the whole class takes an exam. In this study the pattern was implemented over 4 weeks and 12 course hours in a 7th-grade social studies unit.
requirements: Students are divided into groups of 3-7 people, with topics distributed to each group and then redistributed individually within the group
constraints: The article notes the technique becomes effective "to the extent that the teacher has a good grasp of this method and the physical conditions of the classrooms are appropriate for the technique"
target_learning_goals: Social studies content knowledge in the "science through time" unit, including contributions of early civilizations and of Turkish-Islamic scholars to scientific development
examples: In the study, lesson plans were prepared for the jigsaw technique, students were informed about the implementation, separated into equal groups, and subjects were distributed to groups
key_sources: Harun Er. (2017). The Impact of Teaching the Subjects under "Science in Time" Unit in the Social Studies Class in the 7th Grade Using Jigsaw Technique on the Academic Success of the Students. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(5): 838-847. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050516

article_title: The Effects of Using Jigsaw Method Based on Cooperative Learning Model in the Undergraduate Science Laboratory Practices
citation: Ataman Karacop. (2017). The Effects of Using Jigsaw Method Based on Cooperative Learning Model in the Undergraduate Science Laboratory Practices. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(3): 420-434. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050314
title: Jigsaw cooperative learning structure of shared responsibility and expert teaching
description: The article describes Jigsaw as a cooperative learning technique in which "Each team member is responsible for a part of the subject", which the article calls "the main difference between the jigsaw and other cooperative learning methods". This interdependence forces every member to participate actively, so each group member learns the concepts in focus. The technique brings cooperation to the forefront by supporting students working together and removing competition, and it can be used for both theoretical teaching and laboratory experiments.
requirements: Tasks based on no predetermined answers so individuals must cooperate for learning to become meaningful
Learning environments that let students reflect ideas and discuss learning with friends and teachers
constraints: The article notes cooperative learning is not sufficient for understanding especially microscopic-level topics, and too many topics in cooperative groups can make it as ineffective as traditional methods
target_learners: students from elementary school to university level across science, language, social sciences and medical science areas
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
development of social skills and communication between students with different learning histories
examples: In the study, each Jigsaw Group member taught their expert subtopic to group members and shared the experiment procedures carried out in their Expert Group
key_sources: Ataman Karacop. (2017). The Effects of Using Jigsaw Method Based on Cooperative Learning Model in the Undergraduate Science Laboratory Practices. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(3): 420-434. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050314

article_title: Effect of Jigsaw II, Reading-Writing-Presentation, and Computer Animations on the Teaching of "Light" Unit
citation: Koç, Y., Yildiz, E., Çaliklar, Ş., & Şimşek, Ü. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw II, reading-writing-presentation, and computer animations on the teaching of “Light” Unit. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2861
title: Jigsaw II cooperative learning with expert groups and proficiency exams
description: The Jigsaw II technique divides a unit into sub-topics, forms heterogeneous original groups, then gathers students studying the same sub-topic into expert groups. A distinguishing feature is that expert groups take a proficiency exam before returning to teach their peers in original groups. The article used this pattern over five weeks to teach the Light unit, with students researching sub-topics, preparing reports, teaching peers, and making group presentations.
requirements: Heterogeneous original groups formed taking pretest scores and gender into account
Students must be motivated to study together for effective implementation
target_learning_goals: science unit content knowledge (Light unit)
epistemological beliefs
retention of knowledge
examples: The Light unit was divided into four sub-titles: Absorption of Light, Seeing Objects Colorful, Refraction of Light, and Lenses.
key_sources: Koç, Y., Yildiz, E., Çaliklar, Ş., & Şimşek, Ü. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw II, reading-writing-presentation, and computer animations on the teaching of “Light” Unit. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2861

article_title: The Effects of Jigsaw Learning on Students' Attitudes in a Vietnamese Higher Education Classroom
citation: Tran, V. D., & Lewis, R. (2012). The Effects of Jigsaw Learning on Students' Attitudes in a Vietnamese Higher Education Classroom. International Journal of Higher Education, 1(2), 9. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v1n2p9
title: Jigsaw learning implemented through an eight-step procedure with home groups and expert jigsaw groups
description: The article describes a concrete eight-step implementation of jigsaw learning in a higher education course: identifying objectives, organizing materials, forming ten home groups of four and eight jigsaw groups of five, explaining the process with each student assigned a different subunit, moving to jigsaw groups where five students help each other learn one of four subunits, returning to home groups to teach members, and assessing through whole-class presentations. This cycle was 'repeated six times, once for each unit of work.'
requirements: Groups should be small when students begin learning together to help them develop learning skills
constraints: The procedure involved the formation of permanent groups for the duration of a six-week course, which some students reported caused them to lose motivation.
target_learners: final-year undergraduate students in a Vietnamese higher education institution
target_learning_goals: mastering subject-matter content in a Managing Administration and Education course
developing cooperative learning skills
examples: The instructor formed ten home groups of four students and eight jigsaw groups of five, assigned each student a different subunit, had students learn their subunit in jigsaw groups, then return to home groups to teach what they learned, with understanding assessed through whole-class presentations.
key_sources: Tran, V. D., & Lewis, R. (2012). The Effects of Jigsaw Learning on Students' Attitudes in a Vietnamese Higher Education Classroom. International Journal of Higher Education, 1(2), 9. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v1n2p9

article_title: The effect of collaborative learning approach on nursing students' knowledge and skill learning for enteral nutrition: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Acun Aysun, Aksoy Bulgurcu Rahime. (2026). The effect of collaborative learning approach on nursing students' knowledge and skill learning for enteral nutrition: a randomized controlled study. BMC Medical Education 26:328. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08687-w
title: Three-session Jigsaw implementation for enteral nutrition nursing education
description: This element is the concrete collaborative learning implementation the trial used. The article states "The study applied the Jigsaw technique as a collaborative learning method": after three 45-minute lectures, students were randomly divided into five groups of nine, each assigned one enteral nutrition topic (e.g., "insertion and correct fixation of a nasogastric catheter"); groups prepared, practiced, and demonstrated skills over four days in laboratory conditions (14 h total), using role play, demonstration with models, lecture, and question-answer; finally, one student per group transferred knowledge to other groups. Within each group, each member carried out steps of the process and monitored the work done.
requirements: Students randomly divided into groups with a randomly selected spokesperson per group
Topic headings assigned per group covering distinct aspects of enteral nutrition
Laboratory conditions for skill demonstration and observation
constraints: The article notes "the small number of teaching staff in this study presented some disadvantages" and that "Teaching staff had to allocate time to each group in turn"
target_learning_goals: Enteral nutrition knowledge and nursing skills, including nasogastric catheter insertion, administration, and storage of enteral nutrition
examples: Five groups of nine students worked on separate enteral nutrition topics over four consecutive days (4 h on days one to three, 2 h on day four), then group spokespersons shared knowledge across groups.
key_sources: Acun Aysun, Aksoy Bulgurcu Rahime. (2026). The effect of collaborative learning approach on nursing students' knowledge and skill learning for enteral nutrition: a randomized controlled study. BMC Medical Education 26:328. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08687-w

article_title: The Jigsaw teaching method compared to traditional teaching on anatomy and physiology knowledge in higher education - a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Stokstad JM, Nedrehagen ES, Hufthammer KO. (2026). The Jigsaw teaching method compared to traditional teaching on anatomy and physiology knowledge in higher education – a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 26:252. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08608-x
title: The Jigsaw teaching method: structured cooperative learning through expert and primary groups
description: The Jigsaw method is a student-centred cooperative learning structure in which "A central topic is first divided into sub-topics". Students first work in primary groups where each member is assigned a unique sub-topic, then reorganise into expert groups that deepen understanding of one sub-topic, and finally return to their primary groups to teach their sub-topic to peers, so that "the students collectively cover the full topic". In this trial, JS was implemented with expert groups preparing 12-minute presentations for their primary groups, with lecturer facilitation.
requirements: Groups structured so each member is assigned a unique sub-topic and expert groups contain one representative from each primary group
Access to learning resources for expert-group study, and lecturer facilitation and moderation of presentation timing
constraints: The article notes the impact of JS on learning "appears to be context-dependent" with inconsistent effects across settings, and cites evidence that JS may be better suited to less challenging topics
target_learners: undergraduate higher-education students, here social nursing students
target_learning_goals: factual and conceptual knowledge of anatomy and physiology curriculum sub-topics
oral presentation and communication skills
examples: In the trial, five sensory-apparatus sub-topics (sight, hearing, smell and proprioception, touch including pain, taste and equilibrioception) were distributed among primary groups of five students, with 12-minute expert presentations
key_sources: Stokstad JM, Nedrehagen ES, Hufthammer KO. (2026). The Jigsaw teaching method compared to traditional teaching on anatomy and physiology knowledge in higher education – a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 26:252. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08608-x

article_title: Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods.
citation: Laughlin Jacob L. BS, Johnson Lianne R. MS, Ghanekar Bhargav MS, O'Malley Marcia K. PhD. (2025). Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods. Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal. https://doi.org/10.14797/mdcvj.1667
title: JIGSAWS dataset for surgical gesture and skill assessment
description: The JHU-ISI Gesture and Skill-Assessment Working Set (JIGSAWS) is the most widely used benchmark for automated surgical skill assessment. It "includes synchronized videos and kinematic recordings of dry lab surgical tasks—specifically knot tying, needle passing, and suturing—along with self-reported skill levels and mOSATS scores." Researchers use it to train models for skill-level classification (novice/expert or ternary) and mOSATS score regression judged by Spearman correlation. The review reports most automated assessment works were developed on it.
requirements: Supervised models need the dataset's synchronized video, kinematic recordings, and expert grading as ground truth
constraints: A small number of study participants
Low-resolution video quality
target_learners: surgical trainees performing dry lab tasks
target_learning_goals: automated prediction of surgical skill level and mOSATS scores
key_sources: Laughlin Jacob L. BS, Johnson Lianne R. MS, Ghanekar Bhargav MS, O'Malley Marcia K. PhD. (2025). Technical Skills Assessment in Robotic Surgery: A Review of Recent Methods. Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal. https://doi.org/10.14797/mdcvj.1667

article_title: The effects of flipped classroom and jigsaw teaching strategies on learning, retention of course content, and satisfaction among nursing students: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Khodadadeh Alireza, Rivaz Mozhgan, Torabizadeh Camellia. (2025). The effects of flipped classroom and jigsaw teaching strategies on learning, retention of course content, and satisfaction among nursing students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07662-1
title: Jigsaw implementation structure with home groups, expert groups, and QR-coded booklet sections
description: The article implements jigsaw as a cooperative learning structure in which students are "randomly divided into six-person home groups", each member studies one of six booklet sections (with QR codes linking to images and videos), regroups into specialized expert groups to discuss the same content, then returns to the home group where each member has 5 minutes to teach their section, ending with a researcher summary. It was run over four sessions with content, resources, instructor, and tests held constant across groups.
requirements: An educational booklet divided into sections matching the number of group members
A leader for each home group and a researcher acting as supervisor during expert-group discussion
constraints: The authors note implementation challenges reported in prior work including high cognitive load on students, the need for strong collaboration skills, and difficulty ensuring balanced group dynamics
target_learning_goals: learning and retention of medical-surgical nursing course content
examples: Six-person home groups with numbered members studied assigned booklet sections for 10 minutes, met in expert groups for 10 minutes, then taught their content back in home groups
key_sources: Khodadadeh Alireza, Rivaz Mozhgan, Torabizadeh Camellia. (2025). The effects of flipped classroom and jigsaw teaching strategies on learning, retention of course content, and satisfaction among nursing students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07662-1

article_title: Integrating jigsaw teaching into self-regulated learning instruction: an instructional design to improve nursing students' self-regulated learning.
citation: Chen Yiwen, Song Jiali, Li Mengying, He Huijuan, Wang Xiangrong, Zhou Siyu, Wang Ling. (2025). Integrating jigsaw teaching into self-regulated learning instruction: an instructional design to improve nursing students’ self-regulated learning. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1437265
title: Three-phase jigsaw-SRL instructional cycle: forethought, performance, self-reflection
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern that embeds the jigsaw method inside Zimmerman's three-stage SRL cycle. Each of three teaching cycles moves students through a forethought stage with learning guides and task explanation, a performance stage using "expert groups" and "jigsaw groups" with peer teaching, and a self-reflection stage of "self-assessment, mutual assessment, and learning experience sharing". The article implemented it over 12 class hours (6 online, 6 offline) in a Basic Nursing course.
requirements: Content that can be broken into multiple sub-tasks suitable for expert-group division
Learning resources and guides provided in the forethought stage
constraints: Implemented over only three rounds (12 class hours), which the authors say limited self-management gains
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning ability
learning engagement
clinical nursing knowledge and skills
examples: Three Basic Nursing topics (urination care, blood transfusion reactions, penicillin allergy testing) were taught in three cycles with progressively increasing task difficulty
key_sources: Chen Yiwen, Song Jiali, Li Mengying, He Huijuan, Wang Xiangrong, Zhou Siyu, Wang Ling. (2025). Integrating jigsaw teaching into self-regulated learning instruction: an instructional design to improve nursing students’ self-regulated learning. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1437265

article_title: Comparative study of the effect of two small group discussion teaching methods (Tutorial vs Jigsaw) on academic motivation and achievement of undergraduate dental students - a preliminary study.
citation: Haider Ambreen Khurshid, Rehman Javeria, Ali Syeda Kauser. (2025). Comparative study of the effect of two small group discussion teaching methods (Tutorial vs Jigsaw) on academic motivation and achievement of undergraduate dental students – a preliminary study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07244-1
title: Jigsaw small-group discussion method with expert and home groups for undergraduate dental Oral Biology sessions
description: The Jigsaw method is a cooperative small-group discussion technique that, as the article describes it, "emphasizes cooperative learning, where students work in groups to master content and teach each other and to achieve a common goal". In this study it was implemented across three Oral Biology sessions: home groups of five students each prepared assigned portions of a topic, met in same-content expert groups, then regrouped so each student taught peers their portion while the facilitator supervised.
requirements: Facilitators were oriented before implementation: a workshop was conducted "to orient the teachers/facilitators of the Oral Biology Department with the concept of jigsaw method and to train them in conducting it effectively".
constraints: A student comment cautioned that "Jigsaw is a new method which only works if other group members study well."
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
academic achievement in basic dental sciences (Oral Biology)
examples: Students in five home groups (a-e) prepared assigned learning objectives, discussed main learning points in expert groups during the initial 20 minutes of class time, then spent the second half of the session teaching their home-group peers.
key_sources: Haider Ambreen Khurshid, Rehman Javeria, Ali Syeda Kauser. (2025). article_title: Comparative study of the effect of two small group discussion teaching methods (Tutorial vs Jigsaw) on academic motivation and achievement of undergraduate dental students - a preliminary study.

title: Use the jigsaw method in settings with restricted faculty and resources because it requires fewer facilitators than tutorials
description: This principle holds that the Jigsaw methodology is "especially helpful in settings with a restricted number of faculty members and resources because it requires fewer facilitators", with the facilitator supervising rather than leading discussion. The article positions jigsaw as an alternative to tutorials, which it describes as costly, resource-intensive, dependent on highly trained tutors, and prone to devolving into didactic sessions with one student dominating.
requirements: Facilitators need orientation or training in the method; the study ran a workshop beforehand "to orient the teachers/facilitators of the Oral Biology Department with the concept of jigsaw method and to train them in conducting it effectively".
constraints: A student comment cautioned that "Jigsaw is a new method which only works if other group members study well."
target_learners: undergraduate dental students in resource-constrained institutions
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
academic achievement
examples: In this study one facilitator monitored the jigsaw sub-groups while students taught one another, and the authors note the method's advantages for settings with few faculty members.

article_title: Exploring peer learning module vs. conventional tutorials: effects on engagement and learning outcomes among first-year medical students.
citation: Vinay AV, Sindhu R, Rasalkar K. (2025). Exploring peer learning module vs. conventional tutorials: effects on engagement and learning outcomes among first-year medical students. BMC Medical Education 25:101. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06549-x
title: Jigsaw peer learning as a social-constructivist, student-centred alternative to teacher-led tutorials
description: The article frames the peer learning module (PLM) as a student-centric strategy grounded in a social constructivism model in which students "actively construct knowledge by interacting with peers". Its instantiation, the jigsaw technique, gives each member a particular piece of learning material to master and then teach to peers, promoting accountability, collaboration and communication. The article positions PLM against conventional tutorials within a shift from educator-centred to learner-centred medical education under CBME requirements for interactive sessions.
requirements: Small groups with each member responsible for mastering and explaining an assigned subtopic
A faculty member acting as facilitator rather than lecturer
constraints: Requires adequate time; students reported less time for discussion than tutorials
Depends on every member explaining effectively; a failed explanation leaves peers with knowledge gaps
target_learning_goals: physiology conceptual knowledge
communication and teamwork skills
active participation and engagement
examples: Students read and deliberated a subtopic handout for 20 minutes in expert groups, then regrouped and each explained their concept for 8–9 minutes, followed by a randomly chosen student summarizing for 20 minutes
key_sources: Vinay AV, Sindhu R, Rasalkar K. (2025). Exploring peer learning module vs. conventional tutorials: effects on engagement and learning outcomes among first-year medical students. BMC Medical Education 25:101. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06549-x

article_title: Improving emergency medicine resident pediatric lumbar puncture procedural performance through a brief just-in-time video intervention.
citation: McGuire SS, Finch AS, Thomas JM, Lazaro O, Hevesi SA, Mullan AF, Homme JL. (2024). Improving emergency medicine resident pediatric lumbar puncture procedural performance through a brief just-in-time video intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05654-1
title: Brief (4.25-minute) LP instructional video demonstrating the published checklist's major steps
description: A brief instructional video designed and filmed by two of the authors to demonstrate the major steps of the previously published LP Performance Scoring Checklist. The article states that "S.M. and O.L. designed and filmed a brief (4.25 min) instructional LP procedure video [8] that demonstrated the checklist's major steps (Table 1)". It was filmed in about two hours in the ED, edited over approximately six hours, and distributed by email and the department's Intranet Education webpage.
requirements: Based on a previously published, validated procedural scoring checklist so agreed-upon elements of competence are demonstrated
constraints: The authors note the previously published generalized LP checklist may not maintain its validation for assessing performance on a simulated infant patient
target_learning_goals: Procedural competence and efficiency in infant lumbar puncture
examples: Filmed over a two-hour session with a Sony Alpha camera and edited with Wondershare Filmora; distributed via email in March and uploaded to the department Intranet

article_title: Improving emergency medicine resident pediatric lumbar puncture procedural performance through a brief just-in-time video intervention.
citation: McGuire SS, Finch AS, Thomas JM, Lazaro O, Hevesi SA, Mullan AF, Homme JL. (2024). Improving emergency medicine resident pediatric lumbar puncture procedural performance through a brief just-in-time video intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05654-1
title: Use brief checklist-based JIT videos to standardize demonstration of rare-procedure competence independent of supervising physician availability
description: The article argues that pairing a previously published checklist with a brief just-in-time video makes procedural teaching reliable and supervisor-independent: "By utilizing a previously published checklist in a brief JIT video, we ensure that agreed-upon elements of procedural competence are reliably demonstrated to the trainee independent of the supervising physician's time, attention, or skill in teaching". It may also cognitively offload the supervising physician during clinical shifts.
requirements: A previously published, validated procedural checklist as the video's basis
Distribution channels (email, intranet) so trainees can access the video at the point of need
constraints: The authors state future research is needed to determine whether supervising physicians perceive benefits of such JIT resources
Prior more rigorous JIT LP studies demonstrated equivocal success
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents; supervising physicians as secondary users
target_learning_goals: Competence in rare or decreasing-frequency procedures such as pediatric lumbar puncture
examples: The Mayo Clinic EM department created and distributed a 4.25-minute LP video built on the Lammers et al. checklist and used it just-in-time before intern assessments
key_sources: McGuire SS, Finch AS, Thomas JM, Lazaro O, Hevesi SA, Mullan AF, Homme JL. (2024). Improving emergency medicine resident pediatric lumbar puncture procedural performance through a brief just-in-time video intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05654-1

article_title: Just-in-Time In Situ Simulation Training as a Preparedness Measure for the Perioperative Care of COVID-19 Patients.
citation: Zucco Liana MBBS, Chen Michael J. BS, Levy Nadav MD, Obeidat Salameh S. MD, Needham Matthew J. BM BCh, Hyatt Allison MD, Keane Jeffrey R. RN, Pollard Richard J. MD, Mitchell John D. MD, Ramachandran Satya Krishna MD. (2022). Just-in-Time In Situ Simulation Training as a Preparedness Measure for the Perioperative Care of COVID-19 Patients. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000635
title: Use JIT in situ simulation as a preparedness measure for implementing urgent workflow changes during public health crises
description: The article concludes that "JIT, in situ simulation training as a preparedness measure for the perioperative care of COVID-19 patients" demonstrates value during public health crises. Just-in-time training refreshes knowledge and skills for infrequently performed high-risk activities, and in situ delivery in the actual work environment reveals site-specific latent hazards and error-proofs processes while building a shared mental model among interprofessional teams.
requirements: Training content centered on newly produced guidelines staff are expected to perform
Delivery in close temporal and spatial proximity to the clinical encounter
A feedback loop (daily debriefings) connecting simulation findings back to organizational SOP revision
constraints: The article states its findings do not prove causality for the observed low infection rates
Site-specific issues limit generalizability: staff at other facilities reported needing to adjust protocols and retrain local teams
target_learning_goals: safe adoption of redesigned high-risk clinical workflows under time pressure
examples: The program was subsequently adapted into a hospital network-wide simulation training program approved by CRICO, with revised refresh modules for anticipated future COVID-19 surges.
